script.opening: "The midwife and then the doctor at his check said one of Rory’s testicles isn’t where it should be — it’s not in the sac. I’ve been really worried. Is it serious? Does he need an operation? Will it affect him having children one day? I just want to know he’ll be okay."

facts.text: Mother, Laura, on video holding Rory (8 weeks), who is content and feeding well.

Midwife at birth: "the left one isn’t down yet, it might come down". GP at the 8-week check last week: "still not down — it’s in the red book". Laura isn’t sure whether a referral was made. The right side was "fine". Nothing else was said to be wrong with his private parts; he wees from the tip and the stream looks normal.
The left side of the scrotum looks flatter and smaller. She has never felt the testicle there, even in the warm bath. No lump in the groin she has seen.

Born at 38 weeks, 3.2 kg, normal delivery. Feeding well (bottle), gaining weight, no vomiting, no fevers. No groin swelling, never been distressed with a swollen or red scrotum. No medicines, no allergies.
First child. Partner, Josh, works away a lot. Josh’s brother "had an operation for something like this as a boy" and has children.

Anxious, tired new mum; many questions at once. Calm down if the doctor explains clearly that it is common and fixable. Ask: "Does he need a scan first?", "What does the operation involve? He’s so small," and "Could it come down by itself?" Agree readily to him being examined at the surgery and referred.

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "I keep thinking he’ll need a big operation, and that he won’t be able to have children." She has read online about cancer and is frightened to ask.
ice.expectations: "To know what it is and what happens next."

cues: "Will it affect him having children one day?" — fertility worry needing honest, balanced information.
"I’m not sure if anyone referred him" — the referral may have been missed.
"He’s so small" — fear about surgery in a baby.

checkpoints.text: EXAMINES properly, face to face — warm room, warm hands, relaxed/warm child (avoiding cremasteric retraction) — establishing whether the testis is in the scrotum, palpable in the inguinal canal, or impalpable, and examines both sides and the genitalia

Distinguishes a RETRACTILE testis (brought to the bottom of the scrotum without tension and stays — usually benign, yearly review until puberty) from a TRUE UNDESCENDED testis, avoiding both over-referral and missing a genuine UDT

Recognises the must-not-miss urgent presentations — bilateral undescended testes at the newborn check (senior paediatric review within 24 hours), any undescended testis with hypospadias/atypical genitalia (same-day paediatrics for a disorder of sex development/endocrine cause), and acute pain or swelling (possible torsion — emergency)

Knows the REFERRAL pathway and TIMING — still undescended at the 6–8-week check → refer now (NIPE), with no ultrasound first, for ORCHIDOPEXY ideally at 6–12 months and by 18 months at the latest (earlier improves fertility) — and that an acquired/ascending testis also needs surgical referral
COUNSELS the long-term importance proportionately — impaired fertility and increased (harder-to-detect) testicular-cancer risk, hence timely orchidopexy and later testicular self-examination
Reassures the anxious parent proportionately (common, often resolves/correctable, good outlook with timely treatment) and addresses the "will he be okay/fertility/surgery" questions directly
Explains the diagnosis and plan clearly and sensitively, checking understanding without alarming

Safety-nets and follows up: refers now per the NIPE pathway and offers a way to chase it, urgent assessment if bilateral/DSD features, A&E for sudden pain, inconsolable crying or groin/scrotal swelling (torsion), clear timing for orchidopexy, fertility/cancer-risk counselling, and parental support — proper examination + timely referral, not watchful inaction

worked.txt: "Thank you for bringing him — this is common and very treatable, so let’s take it step by step. First I’d like to see him in person and examine him gently in a warm room with warm hands while he’s relaxed, because the cold can make a testicle pop up and look missing when it isn’t. Let me check both sides."

"There are two pictures. Sometimes the testicle can be gently coaxed into the sac and stays — that’s a ‘retractile’ testicle, which is usually harmless and just needs keeping an eye on. If it genuinely won’t come down and stay, that’s a true undescended testicle that needs the surgeons. If it’s retractile, I’d check it once a year."

"His other testicle is normally down, which is reassuring — it’s when BOTH can’t be felt, or there are other differences such as where he wees from, that we’d need an urgent specialist look the same day. That’s not the case here."

"Some come down on their own early on, but because it’s still up at his eight-week check, I’ll refer him to the children’s surgeons now for a small operation called orchidopexy that places and fixes it in the sac — ideally done between six and twelve months, and by eighteen months at the latest, because the timing helps protect his future fertility. He doesn’t need a scan first — it wouldn’t change what the surgeon does."

"To answer your fertility question honestly: leaving it undescended long-term can affect fertility and slightly raises the future risk of a testicular problem, which is exactly why we treat it in good time and why, when he’s older, he’ll be taught to check himself. With timely surgery the outlook is good."

"So: I’m referring him now, and please call us if you haven’t heard within a few weeks. Go to A&E straight away if he has sudden pain, cries inconsolably, or you notice swelling or redness in his groin or scrotum. If you ever notice the other side change, or any concerns, come back. You did the right thing bringing him — he’s going to be well looked after."

f.learning: UNDESCENDED TESTIS (CRYPTORCHIDISM) presents when a testis is not palpable in the scrotum — found at the newborn/6–8-week checks or noticed by a parent — and the first task is to EXAMINE properly, face to face, in a warm room with warm hands and a relaxed, warm child (cold or anxiety triggers the cremasteric reflex and can mimic an undescended testis), establishing whether the testis is in the scrotum, PALPABLE in the inguinal canal (and gently manipulable), or truly IMPALPABLE, examining both sides and the genitalia. The key distinction is between a RETRACTILE testis — which can be brought to the bottom of the scrotum without tension and STAYS there at least briefly, is usually benign, needs no surgery and is reviewed yearly until puberty because some later ascend — and a TRUE UNDESCENDED testis, which cannot be brought into/kept in the scrotum; this avoids both over-referral and missing a genuine UDT. The must-not-misses are BILATERAL undescended testes at the newborn check (senior paediatric review within 24 hours, NIPE) and ANY undescended testis with hypospadias, micropenis, bifid scrotum or atypical genitalia, which may indicate a disorder of sex development or endocrine cause (e.g. congenital adrenal hyperplasia) and needs SAME-DAY paediatric assessment; acute groin or abdominal pain with an undescended testis is possible torsion needing immediate emergency surgical assessment (GIRFT/BAUS pathway). On the pathway and timing (NHS NIPE): a testis still undescended at the 6–8-week check, or found later, is referred NOW to paediatric surgery or urology, with no ultrasound first (it does not reliably locate the testis or change the need for surgical assessment), for ORCHIDOPEXY (surgical placement/fixation in the scrotum) ideally at 6–12 months and by 18 months at the latest (EAU/ESPU 2026, international) — timing matters because earlier surgery improves fertility outcomes, and spontaneous descent after about 6 months (corrected age) is uncommon — and an acquired/ascending testis (previously descended, now undescended) also needs surgical referral. Counsel parents honestly but proportionately that a persistently undescended testis is associated with impaired FERTILITY and an increased, harder-to-detect risk of TESTICULAR CANCER, which is why timely orchidopexy (reducing but not removing the cancer risk; Pettersson, NEJM 2007) and, from puberty, testicular SELF-AWARENESS are advised — framing this as the reason for treatment, not alarm. Reassure proportionately (it is common, often resolves or is correctable, with a good outlook after timely treatment), explain the plan, support the anxious parent, and safety-net.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NHS Newborn and Infant Physical Examination (NIPE) screening programme · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] EAU/ESPU guidelines on paediatric urology (2026, international) · [4] GIRFT/BAUS children and young people testicular torsion pathway (2026) · [5] Pettersson et al., NEJM 2007 (orchidopexy age and testicular cancer risk)
knowledge.summary: A testis still not in the scrotum at the 6–8-week check should be referred to paediatric surgery or urology now, so orchidopexy can be done ideally at 6–12 months and by 18 months at the latest. Examine properly to separate a retractile testis, screen for the urgent presentations, do not request an ultrasound, and counsel honestly about fertility and later testicular awareness.

points.t: Bilateral impalpable testes, or a unilateral impalpable testis, at the newborn check: senior paediatric review within 24 hours [1]. Any undescended testis with hypospadias, micropenis, bifid scrotum or atypical genitalia: same-day paediatrics for possible disorder of sex development, including congenital adrenal hyperplasia [1][2]. Acute groin or abdominal pain with an undescended testis: possible torsion, immediate emergency surgical assessment [4].

Warm room, warm hands, relaxed child, supine and then frog-legged. Sweep from the groin down. Note whether the testis is palpable, the other testis, the penis and urethral opening, the scrotum, and any hernia.

Can the testis be brought to the bottom of the scrotum without tension, and does it stay at least briefly? Yes: retractile, no surgery, review yearly because some ascend. No, or springs straight back: undescended. If unsure, refer [2].

Unilateral palpable at the newborn check: re-examine at 6–8 weeks and, if needed, at 4–5 months (corrected age). Bilateral at 6–8 weeks: urgent paediatric referral, seen within 2 weeks. Still undescended, now impalpable, or found later: refer to paediatric surgery or urology per the local NIPE pathway, aiming for specialist review by 6 months [1]. Spontaneous descent after about 6 months (corrected age) is uncommon [2].

Ideally at 6–12 months, and by 18 months at the latest [2]. Earlier surgery gives the testis the best chance for later fertility, and orchidopexy before puberty is associated with a lower testicular cancer risk than later surgery [5].

Imaging does not reliably find a non-palpable testis and does not change the need for surgical assessment. Refer directly; a scan request can delay treatment [2]. A non-palpable testis is assessed by the surgeon, often with laparoscopy.
A testis that was in the scrotum can ascend with growth. Treat it as undescended and refer when found.

A history of undescended testis raises the risk of subfertility and testicular cancer; orchidopexy reduces but does not remove the cancer risk. From puberty he should know how his testes normally feel and report any change. In adults, NICE NG12 testicular criteria apply [3].

True undescended versus retractile, ascending or absent testis; DSD if bilateral or atypical genitalia; hernia.

Unilateral undescended testis, still present at the 6–8-week check.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Morgan. And this must be Rory. What’s been happening?

The midwife and then the doctor at his check said one of Rory’s testicles isn’t where it should be. It’s not in the sac. I’ve been really worried. Is it serious? Does he need an operation? Will it affect him having children one day? I just want to know he’ll be okay.
Those are really important questions and I’ll answer each of them. First, this is common and very treatable. Can I ask a few things, examine him gently, and then we’ll go through what happens next?
Yes, please.
Was he born around his due date or early? Babies born early can take a bit longer for the testicles to come down.
I’m not sure of the exact weeks. It’s in his red book.
Thank you, I’ll check. Did they mention anything else at his checks, for example about where his wee comes out, or the other side?
model.why: Screens hypospadias and the other testis

model.text: They said the other side was fine. Nothing else.
Has he seemed in pain, cried a lot when his nappy is changed, or have you seen any swelling in his groin?
No, he’s been fine. Feeding well.
What’s been going through your mind since they told you?
I keep thinking something’s wrong with him, that he’ll need an operation, and that he won’t be able to have children.
That’s a lot to carry, especially with a new baby. What would help most today?
Knowing what it is and what happens next.

I’ll warm my hands and examine him while he’s relaxed, because cold or crying can make a testicle pop up out of the sac … His penis looks normal and the opening is in the right place. The other testicle is down in the sac. On the other side, I’m gently trying to bring it down to the bottom of the sac and see if it stays.
model.why: Warm, relaxed examination; genitalia; mobility test

model.text: And?

It isn’t coming down and staying in the sac today. There are two possibilities with this. Sometimes a testicle is just pulled up by a muscle and can be brought down and stays, which we call retractile, and that doesn’t need an operation. Today it isn’t behaving like that, so it’s what we call an undescended testicle: it hasn’t finished its journey down before birth.
Is that serious?

It’s common and it isn’t dangerous for him now. The reassuring things are that his other testicle is down and everything else looks normal. If both couldn’t be felt, or there were other differences, we’d want a specialist to see him urgently. That isn’t the case.
model.why: Bilateral or atypical genitalia red flag, stated as absent

model.text: Because it’s still up at his eight-week check, the guidance is to refer him now to the children’s surgeons, rather than wait. Some do come down in the first few months, and the surgeons will check again. If it’s still up, they do a small operation called an orchidopexy to bring it down and fix it in the sac, ideally between six months and his first birthday.
model.why: Refers now on the NIPE timetable; orchidopexy timing

model.text: Does he need a scan first?
No. Scans aren’t good at finding these and they don’t change what the surgeon needs to do, so a scan would only delay things. The surgeon will examine him and decide.
And having children, is that affected?

An honest answer: a testicle left up long-term can affect fertility, and it slightly raises the chance of a testicular problem, including cancer, later in life. That’s exactly why we treat it in good time. With the operation in the first year, the outlook is good. When he’s older, we’ll teach him to check himself, as all young men should.
model.why: Balanced fertility and cancer counselling; later self-examination

model.text: What does the operation involve? He’s so small.

It’s usually a day-case operation under a general anaesthetic, through a small cut in the groin or scrotum, and most babies go home the same day. The surgeons will explain it fully and answer your questions before anything is decided.
model.why: Explains the operation simply and defers detail to the specialist

model.text: And could it come down by itself before then?
It can in the first few months, and if it does the surgeons will simply discharge him. Referring now doesn’t commit him to an operation; it makes sure he’s seen in time if it doesn’t come down.
model.why: Explains that referral now protects the surgical window

model.text: Okay. That actually makes me feel better, knowing there’s a plan.

One important thing: if he ever seems in sudden pain, is inconsolable, or you see a swelling or redness in his groin or scrotum, take him to A&E straight away, because a testicle that hasn’t come down can occasionally twist. Also, if you notice a change on the other side, let us know. I’ll send the referral today. Can you tell me what you’ll tell anyone at home tonight?
model.why: Torsion safety-net, referral today and teach-back

model.text: It’s common, one hasn’t come down, he’s being referred to the children’s surgeons for a small operation in his first year, no scan needed, and A&E if he’s in sudden pain or there’s swelling.
Perfect. You did exactly the right thing bringing him. If you haven’t heard about the appointment in a few weeks, call us and we’ll chase it.
model.why: Confirms understanding; closes the referral loop

social.t: New parents often fear the worst after screening findings. Clear explanation, a named plan and a way to chase the referral reduce anxiety.
Day-case surgery in the first year; explain that the surgical team will give instructions on feeding, pain relief and follow-up.

legal.t: A person with parental responsibility consents to surgery for an infant. GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018): involve parents in decisions and act in the child’s best interests.
The NIPE programme sets referral standards; record the examination findings and the referral clearly.

professional.t: Missed or delayed referrals are a known cause of late orchidopexy. Use a safety-netting system to confirm the appointment is made.
Answer fertility and cancer questions honestly without precise-sounding numbers; avoid both false reassurance and alarm.

community.t: The health visitor can support the family, reinforce the plan and check the referral has progressed.

redFlags: Bilateral impalpable testes (senior paediatric review; possible DSD or CAH)
Hypospadias, micropenis, bifid scrotum or atypical genitalia (same-day paediatrics)
Sudden groin or abdominal pain, inconsolable crying, groin or scrotal swelling (possible torsion: A&E)
Testis previously down now not (ascending testis: refer)
psychosocial: Maternal anxiety with a new baby
ice: Idea: something is wrong with him
Concern: an operation and his future fertility
Expectation: to know what it is and what happens next

playbook.diagnosis: “One of Rory’s testicles hasn’t finished coming down into the sac. It’s called an undescended testicle. It’s common and treatable, and everything else looks normal.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Before birth, each testicle travels from the tummy down into the sac. Sometimes one stops partway. It isn’t dangerous now, but it works best in the cooler sac, which is why the surgeons bring it down in his first year.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried something was wrong and about his fertility. This is common, his other testicle and everything else look normal, and treating it in his first year gives him the best outlook.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge a new parent’s anxiety; give a clear, named next step; offer a way to chase the referral; involve the health visitor.
sharedPlan: Refer now to paediatric surgery or urology per the local NIPE pathway
Orchidopexy ideally at 6–12 months, by 18 months at the latest
If a retractile testis is found later, yearly review until puberty
safetyNet: A&E for sudden pain, inconsolable crying, groin or scrotal swelling or redness
Tell us if the other side changes
Call if no appointment within a few weeks

pitfalls.intro: The marks here sit in a proper examination, the right referral at the right time, and honest counselling that calms rather than frightens.

items.why: NIPE and the site’s undescended testis protocol: still undescended at 6–8 weeks means refer now, so surgery happens at 6–12 months.
items.fix: Refer to paediatric surgery or urology today and explain the timing.

items.why: EAU/ESPU: imaging doesn’t reliably locate the testis and delays treatment.
items.fix: Refer directly and explain why no scan is needed.

items.fail: No mobility test, or examining a cold, crying baby.
items.why: A retractile testis can be mislabelled as undescended, or the reverse.
items.fix: Warm hands, relaxed baby, bring it down and see whether it stays.

items.fail: Not looking at the penis and the other side.
items.why: Bilateral impalpable testes or hypospadias change the urgency (possible DSD or CAH).
items.fix: Examine the whole genitalia and state that the red flags are absent.

items.fail: Dodging the fertility question, or answering it with alarming figures.
items.why: She asked directly; evasion or fear both lose marks.
items.fix: Honest and proportionate: why early surgery helps, and later self-examination.

items.fail: No torsion safety-net and no plan to chase the referral.
items.why: Torsion of an undescended testis is easily missed, and referrals get lost.
items.fix: A&E for sudden pain or swelling; call if no appointment arrives.

timeMap.d: Let her ask all her questions; reassure early that it is common and treatable.
Gestation, what was said at the checks, the other side, urethral opening, pain, crying, groin swelling.
Something wrong, an operation, future fertility; wants to know what happens next.
Warm hands, mobility test, genitalia; retractile versus undescended; red flags absent.
Refer now, orchidopexy at 6–12 months, no scan, honest fertility and cancer counselling, torsion safety-net, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Examines a cold, crying baby and makes no mobility test; says “wait and see until he’s one”; requests an ultrasound; either dismisses the fertility question or alarms her about cancer.
wordPics.pass: Examines properly, distinguishes retractile from undescended, checks the genitalia, refers to paediatric surgery on the NIPE timetable, and counsels about fertility.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: names the red flags and states they are absent; explains why no scan; gives orchidopexy timing with the reason; answers fertility and cancer questions honestly without precise-sounding numbers; torsion safety-net; teach-back and a plan to chase the referral.

avoid.dont: “Let’s wait and see until his first birthday.”
avoid.instead: “Because it’s still up at his eight-week check, I’ll refer him to the children’s surgeons now.”
avoid.why: NIPE: still undescended at 6–8 weeks means referral, so surgery can be done at 6–12 months.

avoid.dont: “I’ll send him for an ultrasound to find it.”
avoid.instead: “A scan won’t help find it or change what the surgeon does, so we’ll refer directly.”
avoid.why: EAU/ESPU advise against imaging before referral; it delays treatment.

avoid.dont: “It means he’ll be infertile and could get cancer.”
avoid.instead: “Left untreated it can affect fertility and slightly raise later risks, which is exactly why we treat it early.”
avoid.why: Honest, proportionate counselling informs without frightening.

SCA_MODELS.text: Does he need a scan first?
No. Scans aren’t good at finding these and they don’t change what the surgeon needs to do, so a scan would only delay things. The surgeon will examine him and decide.
And having children, is that affected?

An honest answer: a testicle left up long-term can affect fertility, and it slightly raises the chance of a testicular problem, including cancer, later in life. That’s exactly why we treat it in good time. With the operation in the first year, the outlook is good. When he’s older, we’ll teach him to check himself, as all young men should.
SCA_MODELS.why: Balanced fertility and cancer counselling; later self-examination

SCA_MODELS.text: What does the operation involve? He’s so small.

It’s usually a day-case operation under a general anaesthetic, through a small cut in the groin or scrotum, and most babies go home the same day. The surgeons will explain it fully and answer your questions before anything is decided.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the operation simply and defers detail to the specialist

SCA_MODELS.text: And could it come down by itself before then?
It can in the first few months, and if it does the surgeons will simply discharge him. Referring now doesn’t commit him to an operation; it makes sure he’s seen in time if it doesn’t come down.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains that referral now protects the surgical window

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That actually makes me feel better, knowing there’s a plan.

One important thing: if he ever seems in sudden pain, is inconsolable, or you see a swelling or redness in his groin or scrotum, take him to A&E straight away, because a testicle that hasn’t come down can occasionally twist. Also, if you notice a change on the other side, let us know. I’ll send the referral today. Can you tell me what you’ll tell anyone at home tonight?
SCA_MODELS.why: Torsion safety-net, referral today and teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: It’s common, one hasn’t come down, he’s being referred to the children’s surgeons for a small operation in his first year, no scan needed, and A&E if he’s in sudden pain or there’s swelling.
Perfect. You did exactly the right thing bringing him. If you haven’t heard about the appointment in a few weeks, call us and we’ll chase it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Confirms understanding; closes the referral loop

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NHS Newborn and Infant Physical Examination (NIPE) screening programme · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] EAU/ESPU guidelines on paediatric urology (2026, international) · [4] GIRFT/BAUS children and young people testicular torsion pathway (2026) · [5] Pettersson et al., NEJM 2007 (orchidopexy age and testicular cancer risk)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A testis still not in the scrotum at the 6–8-week check should be referred to paediatric surgery or urology now, so orchidopexy can be done ideally at 6–12 months and by 18 months at the latest. Examine properly to separate a retractile testis, screen for the urgent presentations, do not request an ultrasound, and counsel honestly about fertility and later testicular awareness.

points.t: Bilateral impalpable testes, or a unilateral impalpable testis, at the newborn check: senior paediatric review within 24 hours [1]. Any undescended testis with hypospadias, micropenis, bifid scrotum or atypical genitalia: same-day paediatrics for possible disorder of sex development, including congenital adrenal hyperplasia [1][2]. Acute groin or abdominal pain with an undescended testis: possible torsion, immediate emergency surgical assessment [4].

Warm room, warm hands, relaxed child, supine and then frog-legged. Sweep from the groin down. Note whether the testis is palpable, the other testis, the penis and urethral opening, the scrotum, and any hernia.

Can the testis be brought to the bottom of the scrotum without tension, and does it stay at least briefly? Yes: retractile, no surgery, review yearly because some ascend. No, or springs straight back: undescended. If unsure, refer [2].

Unilateral palpable at the newborn check: re-examine at 6–8 weeks and, if needed, at 4–5 months (corrected age). Bilateral at 6–8 weeks: urgent paediatric referral, seen within 2 weeks. Still undescended, now impalpable, or found later: refer to paediatric surgery or urology per the local NIPE pathway, aiming for specialist review by 6 months [1]. Spontaneous descent after about 6 months (corrected age) is uncommon [2].

Ideally at 6–12 months, and by 18 months at the latest [2]. Earlier surgery gives the testis the best chance for later fertility, and orchidopexy before puberty is associated with a lower testicular cancer risk than later surgery [5].

Imaging does not reliably find a non-palpable testis and does not change the need for surgical assessment. Refer directly; a scan request can delay treatment [2]. A non-palpable testis is assessed by the surgeon, often with laparoscopy.
A testis that was in the scrotum can ascend with growth. Treat it as undescended and refer when found.

A history of undescended testis raises the risk of subfertility and testicular cancer; orchidopexy reduces but does not remove the cancer risk. From puberty he should know how his testes normally feel and report any change. In adults, NICE NG12 testicular criteria apply [3].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let the mother voice all her questions before starting; early proportionate reassurance.
Maternal anxiety with a new baby; who else she will share the plan with.
Picked up “will it affect him having children” and returned to answer it directly.
Idea (something is wrong), concern (operation, fertility), expectation (to know what it is and what happens next).
Warm, relaxed examination; both sides; mobility test; penis, urethral opening and scrotum; groin for hernia. No ultrasound.
True undescended versus retractile, ascending or absent testis; DSD if bilateral or atypical genitalia; hernia.
Bilateral impalpable and atypical genitalia excluded; torsion and hernia symptoms screened.
Unilateral undescended testis, still present at the 6–8-week check.
Refer now to paediatric surgery or urology per the NIPE pathway; orchidopexy ideally at 6–12 months, by 18 months at the latest; no scan.
Balanced counselling on fertility and later testicular cancer risk; later self-examination; maternal reassurance.
A&E for sudden pain, inconsolable crying or groin swelling; report changes on the other side; chase the referral if no appointment; teach-back.

social.t: New parents often fear the worst after screening findings. Clear explanation, a named plan and a way to chase the referral reduce anxiety.
Day-case surgery in the first year; explain that the surgical team will give instructions on feeding, pain relief and follow-up.

legal.t: A person with parental responsibility consents to surgery for an infant. GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018): involve parents in decisions and act in the child’s best interests.
The NIPE programme sets referral standards; record the examination findings and the referral clearly.

professional.t: Missed or delayed referrals are a known cause of late orchidopexy. Use a safety-netting system to confirm the appointment is made.
Answer fertility and cancer questions honestly without precise-sounding numbers; avoid both false reassurance and alarm.

community.t: The health visitor can support the family, reinforce the plan and check the referral has progressed.

redFlags: Bilateral impalpable testes (senior paediatric review; possible DSD or CAH)
Hypospadias, micropenis, bifid scrotum or atypical genitalia (same-day paediatrics)
Sudden groin or abdominal pain, inconsolable crying, groin or scrotal swelling (possible torsion: A&E)
Testis previously down now not (ascending testis: refer)

ice: Idea: something is wrong with him
Concern: an operation and his future fertility
Expectation: to know what it is and what happens next

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “One of Rory’s testicles hasn’t finished coming down into the sac. It’s called an undescended testicle. It’s common and treatable, and everything else looks normal.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Before birth, each testicle travels from the tummy down into the sac. Sometimes one stops partway. It isn’t dangerous now, but it works best in the cooler sac, which is why the surgeons bring it down in his first year.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried something was wrong and about his fertility. This is common, his other testicle and everything else look normal, and treating it in his first year gives him the best outlook.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge a new parent’s anxiety; give a clear, named next step; offer a way to chase the referral; involve the health visitor.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The marks here sit in a proper examination, the right referral at the right time, and honest counselling that calms rather than frightens.

items.why: NIPE and the site’s undescended testis protocol: still undescended at 6–8 weeks means refer now, so surgery happens at 6–12 months.
items.fix: Refer to paediatric surgery or urology today and explain the timing.

items.why: EAU/ESPU: imaging doesn’t reliably locate the testis and delays treatment.
items.fix: Refer directly and explain why no scan is needed.

items.fail: No mobility test, or examining a cold, crying baby.
items.why: A retractile testis can be mislabelled as undescended, or the reverse.
items.fix: Warm hands, relaxed baby, bring it down and see whether it stays.

items.fail: Not looking at the penis and the other side.
items.why: Bilateral impalpable testes or hypospadias change the urgency (possible DSD or CAH).
items.fix: Examine the whole genitalia and state that the red flags are absent.

items.fail: Dodging the fertility question, or answering it with alarming figures.
items.why: She asked directly; evasion or fear both lose marks.
items.fix: Honest and proportionate: why early surgery helps, and later self-examination.

items.fail: No torsion safety-net and no plan to chase the referral.
items.why: Torsion of an undescended testis is easily missed, and referrals get lost.
items.fix: A&E for sudden pain or swelling; call if no appointment arrives.
